body:
Every NBT file Minecraft writes

NBT (Named Binary Tag) is one format with several encodings, and every Minecraft edition, launcher and server core uses a different combination of them. This editor implements all of them and picks the right one from the bytes themselves, so you never have to know which variant a file is before you open it.

FileComes fromEncodingCompression
level.datJava world — Vanilla, Paper, Spigot, Fabric, ForgeBig-endian, named rootgzip
level.datBedrock world — BDS, PocketMine-MP, Nukkit, MCPELittle-endian + 8-byte headerNone
<uuid>.datJava playerdata/Big-endiangzip
servers.dat, hotbar.nbtJava clientBig-endianNone
idcounts.dat, raids.dat, map_*.datJava world data/Big-endiangzip
.nbtStructure blocks, datapack structuresBig-endiangzip
.schem, .schematicWorldEdit, Sponge, MCEditBig-endiangzip
.mcstructureBedrock structure blocksLittle-endianNone
Chunk payloadRegion .mca extract, LevelDB valueEither byte orderzlib or none
Packet dumpBedrock protocol, Java 1.20.2+ protocolVarint LE / nameless BENone

How to edit an NBT file

  1. Get the file off the server or device. Java servers keep it in world/, Bedrock servers in worlds/YourWorld/, Android in games/com.mojang/minecraftWorlds/<id>/. Stop the server first so the file is not being written while you copy it.
  2. Drop it into the editor. The badge above the tree tells you what was detected — edition, encoding, compression and, for Bedrock, the storage version from the header.
  3. Edit. Tap a value to change it in place. Use search to jump to a tag by name or value, + to add tags to any compound or list, × to remove them.
  4. Save & Download. The output format and compression selectors default to whatever the file arrived as, so a plain edit is a byte-faithful round trip.
  5. Put it back and restart. Keep the original as a backup until the world has loaded once and looks right.

What makes this editor different

Five encodings, one drop zone

Java big-endian, Bedrock little-endian, Bedrock varint network NBT, nameless-root network NBT from Java 1.20.2+, and Bedrock's headered level.dat. Detected, not guessed.

gzip and zlib in the browser

Decompression and recompression use the native Compression Streams API, so a Java level.dat round-trips into a file the game accepts unchanged.

Real 64-bit longs

TAG_Long values are held as BigInt. World seeds and UUID halves survive editing instead of being mangled by floating-point rounding, which is where most browser NBT tools break.

Correct string encoding

Java writes modified UTF-8 (CESU-8), Bedrock writes standard UTF-8. The editor encodes per edition, so emoji and non-Latin world names come out intact.

Built for big files

Arrays live in typed arrays and the tree renders lazily, 200 entries at a time. A megabyte of chunk NBT opens without freezing the tab.

Search across the tree

Find any tag by name or value anywhere in the file and jump straight to it with the path expanded.

SNBT export

Dump the whole tree as SNBT — the text form used by /data and datapacks — for diffing, sharing or pasting into a command.

Format conversion

Read a Bedrock file, write Java big-endian gzip, or the reverse. Useful for protocol work, tests and tooling.

Nothing leaves your device

The file is read with FileReader, parsed in JavaScript, and handed back as an in-memory blob. No upload endpoint exists.

Supported server software — all of it

NBT is written by the game, not by the server implementation, so any core that stores a Minecraft world stores it in one of the encodings this editor reads. That is the whole list below, and it is not a marketing list: a core that writes a world writes it in Vanilla's shape, because the client on the other end has to read it.

Bedrock Edition — little-endian NBT, 8-byte level.dat header

Bedrock Dedicated Server (BDS), PocketMine-MP (PM3, PM4, PM5), Nukkit, Nukkit-MOT, PowerNukkitX, Cloudburst Server, Dragonfly, Endstone, LeviLamina and BDSX, Allay, JukeboxMC, GoMint, Sculk, ElementZero, LiteLoaderBDS, plus the MCPE and MCBE clients themselves on Android, iOS, Windows, console and Switch. Same worlds/<World>/level.dat, same header, same tags — see the server-side workflow.

Java Edition — big-endian NBT, gzip

Vanilla, CraftBukkit, Spigot, Paper, Purpur, Pufferfish, Folia, Leaves, Gale, Petal, Airplane, Sponge (SpongeVanilla, SpongeForge), Fabric, Quilt, Forge, NeoForge, Mohist, Arclight, Magma, Ketting, Banner, Cardboard, Glowstone, Thermos, Uberbukkit and every other fork, modpack server or ancient legacy build. If it writes world/level.dat, this editor opens it — details here.

Proxies and bridges

Geyser, WaterdogPE, Waterfall, Velocity and BungeeCord do not own worlds; they move NBT over the wire. Captures from those sockets are network NBT — varint little-endian on the Bedrock side, nameless-root big-endian on Java 1.20.2+ — and both open here directly.

Anything not on this list

Custom forks, private cores, teaching projects, a server you wrote yourself: if the file is NBT, the editor detects which of the five encodings it is and opens it. Nothing here is keyed to a core's name.

Use the parser from your own code

The page exposes its engine on window.NBT, so the same parser that powers the UI can be driven from the browser console or reused in a userscript:

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());
const { root, format, compression, headerVersion } = await NBT.read(bytes);

root.value.find(t => t.name === "LevelName").value = "New World";

const out = await NBT.write(root, format, { compression, headerVersion });

Tags are plain objects — { type, name, value, listType } — arrays are Int8Array, Int32Array and BigInt64Array, and longs are BigInt. The full NBT format reference documents every tag type and how each encoding differs.
faq: Is this NBT editor free?

Yes, and open source under the MIT licence. There is no paid tier, no sign-up and no upload quota, because there is no server component at all — the whole editor is one static page plus two asset files.
Does it work with Java Edition and Bedrock Edition?

Both. Java Edition files are big-endian and usually gzip-compressed; Bedrock files are little-endian, and level.dat carries an extra 8-byte header. The editor detects which one it received and writes the same variant back on save.
Is my world file uploaded anywhere?
No. The file is read locally with the FileReader API and the download is produced from an in-memory blob. Once the page has loaded you can disconnect from the network and it still works.
Can I use it on Android or iOS?

Yes. The layout is mobile-first with 44 px tap targets and a fixed action bar. On Android you can pick a world file straight out of a file manager; on iOS the file has to be in the Files app first because of sandboxing.
What is the difference between NBT and SNBT?

NBT is the binary encoding Minecraft stores on disk. SNBT is its text form, the syntax you type into commands like /data merge. This editor reads binary NBT and can export SNBT, which makes it easy to diff two files or paste a structure into a command.
Which tools does this replace?
Desktop NBT editors such as NBTExplorer, plus the various single-purpose web tools that only handle one edition. See the NBTExplorer online comparison for what carries over and what does not.

level-dat-editor.answer: level.dat is the file that holds everything a Minecraft world knows about itself: its name, game mode, difficulty, spawn point, game rules, weather state and the version it was last opened with. Drop it below to edit any of those values directly. Java files (gzip, big-endian) and Bedrock files (little-endian with an 8-byte header) are both handled, and the file is written back in the format it arrived in.
level-dat-editor.body:
The tags people actually edit

A Java level.dat keeps almost everything inside a single Data compound; a Bedrock level.dat keeps its tags flat at the root. The names below are the ones worth knowing — search for any of them in the tree and the editor will jump to it.

TagTypeEditionWhat it controls
LevelNameStringBothThe world's display name. Stale after copying a world folder — the rename guide covers it.
GameType / gameTypeIntBoth0 survival, 1 creative, 2 adventure, 3 spectator.
DifficultyByte / IntBoth0 peaceful, 1 easy, 2 normal, 3 hard.
hardcoreByteBoth1 locks the world to hardcore rules.
allowCommands / commandsEnabledByteJava / BedrockWhether cheats are enabled.
SpawnX, SpawnY, SpawnZIntBothWorld spawn coordinates.
Time, DayTimeLongJavaTotal ticks and the time of day.
currentTickIntBedrockBedrock's equivalent world clock.
RandomSeed / WorldGenSettings.seedLongJavaWorld seed. Held as a real 64-bit value here, not a rounded double.
GameRules / individual gamerule tagsCompound / ByteJava / BedrockEverything /gamerule sets — see the game rules guide.
DataVersionIntJavaThe world format version. Check it before moving a world between Minecraft versions.
lastOpenedWithVersionList of IntBedrockThe Bedrock client or server build that last wrote the world.
PlayerCompoundBothSingle-player inventory, position and stats embedded in the world file.

Where level.dat lives

PlatformPath

Bedrock Dedicated Server, PocketMine-MP, Nukkitworlds/<World>/level.dat

Minecraft also writes a level.dat_old next to it — the previous save. It opens in this editor too, and it is the first thing to try if the current file will not load.

Editing safely

  • Stop the server or close the game first. Minecraft rewrites level.dat on autosave and on shutdown, and a running server will overwrite your edit — or worse, write over a half-copied file.
  • Keep the original. This editor never modifies the file you dropped in; it produces a new download. Keep the old copy until the world has loaded once.
  • Do not change tag types. Changing Difficulty from Byte to Int, or renaming a tag Minecraft expects, is how a world stops loading. Edit values, not the structure, unless you know why.
  • Keep the Bedrock header intact. The 8-byte header carries the storage version and payload length. The editor rewrites the length automatically and preserves the version; hand-edited files that lose it will not load.
faq: Can I edit level.dat without downloading software?
Yes — that is what this page is. The parser runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install and no operating system requirement beyond a current browser.
Why does my world still show the old name?
Because the name in the world list comes from LevelName inside level.dat, not from the folder name. Copying or renaming a folder leaves the tag untouched. Edit the tag and the list updates.
Does this work with level.dat_old?
Yes. level.dat_old is the previous save in the same format. If the current file is corrupt, open the _old copy, confirm it looks sane, and restore it under the original name.
Can I change the world seed here?

You can edit the seed tag, but it only affects terrain generated after the change — chunks already on disk keep the shape they were generated with, so the join between old and new terrain will be visible.
Will editing level.dat get me banned or corrupt my world?

It is your own save file, so there is nothing to ban. Corruption comes from editing while the server is running, or from changing tag types and names rather than values. Stop the server, edit values, keep a backup.

java-nbt-editor.answer: Minecraft Java Edition stores its data as big-endian NBT, almost always gzip-compressed. Drop any Java file below — level.dat, a playerdata UUID file, servers.dat, a structure .nbt, a WorldEdit schematic — and the editor decompresses it, parses it big-endian and writes it back gzip-compressed so the game accepts it unchanged.
java-nbt-editor.body:
What a Java world is made of

Everything below opens in the editor above. Region files themselves (.mca) are a container of many compressed chunks rather than a single NBT document, so extract a chunk payload first — the editor reads the zlib-compressed chunk NBT that comes out.

PathContentsCompression
world/level.datWorld name, game mode, rules, spawn, DataVersiongzip
world/level.dat_oldPrevious save of the same filegzip
world/playerdata/<uuid>.datInventory, ender chest, position, health, XP, attributesgzip
world/data/raids.dat, idcounts.dat, map_*.datRaid state, entity id counters, map itemsgzip
world/data/scoreboard.datObjectives, teams, scoresgzip
world/region/*.mcaChunk NBT inside a region containerzlib per chunk
servers.datMultiplayer server list from the clientnone
hotbar.nbtSaved creative hotbarsnone
*.nbt in datapacksStructures placed by structure blocks and jigsawsgzip

How Java encodes NBT

  • Big-endian. Every integer and float is stored most-significant byte first, matching Java's DataOutputStream.
  • Named root. The file starts with tag type 0x0A, then a UTF-8 length-prefixed root name — historically empty in level.dat.
  • Modified UTF-8. Strings use Java's writeUTF encoding: a two-byte length, NUL written as C0 80, and characters outside the basic plane split into two three-byte halves (CESU-8). A tool that treats this as plain UTF-8 mangles emoji in world names; this editor encodes it correctly.
  • gzip by default. NbtIo.readCompressed expects a gzip stream. Files written uncompressed load in some tools but not in the game.
  • Nameless root on the network. Since 1.20.2 the protocol sends NBT without the root name. Packet dumps in that shape are detected as Java network here.

Paper, Spigot, Fabric, Forge — same files

Forks and mod loaders change how the server runs, not how the world is written. Paper, Purpur, Pufferfish, Folia, Fabric, Quilt, Forge, NeoForge, Mohist, Arclight and Sponge all use Vanilla's NBT layout, so anything on this page applies to them unchanged. What forks do add is extra files beside the world — paper-world.yml, mod configs — which are YAML or TOML and unrelated to NBT.

Mods and plugins may add their own compounds inside level.dat or playerdata. Those tags open here like any other; leave them alone unless you know what the mod does with them.

DataVersion and version migration

Java worlds carry a DataVersion integer that identifies the world format, incremented on every snapshot. Some useful anchors: 1.16.5 is 2586, 1.17.1 is 2730, 1.18.2 is 2975, 1.19.4 is 3337, 1.20.4 is 3700, 1.21 is 3953. Opening a world in an older client than the one that wrote it is refused precisely because of this tag, and lowering it by hand does not downgrade the chunk data behind it — it just removes the guard rail. Read it to find out what wrote a world; do not edit it to force a downgrade.
faq: Can I open a Java level.dat that will not load in game?

Usually yes — the editor is more tolerant than the game about trailing bytes, and it reports exactly where parsing stopped if the file is truncated. If it refuses too, try level.dat_old, which is the previous autosave.
Does it support 1.20.2+ network NBT?
Yes. From 1.20.2 the protocol omits the root name. A dump in that shape is detected as the Java network format and can be re-saved either as network NBT or as a normal named-root file.
Can I edit a chunk from a .mca region file?

You can edit chunk NBT once it is extracted from the region container. The .mca itself is an index plus many zlib-compressed chunk payloads, and this editor works on a single NBT document, not on the container.
Will editing playerdata break the player?

Only if the server is running while you do it — it holds player state in memory and writes it out on logout, overwriting your file. Take the player offline, edit, then let them reconnect. See the playerdata editor.
Is a gzip level.dat required?
The vanilla loader reads gzip. Save with compression set to gzip — the default when the file arrived that way — and the game will accept it.

mcpe-nbt-editor.body:
The 8-byte header, and why it matters

A Bedrock level.dat is not raw NBT. The first four bytes are a little-endian storage version (8 and 10 are the values in the wild), the next four are the byte length of the NBT payload, and the tags follow uncompressed. Edit the payload without fixing that length and the game rejects the file — which is exactly what happens when people open Bedrock saves in a Java-only NBT tool.

OffsetSizeField
04 bytesStorage version, little-endian int
44 bytesPayload length in bytes, little-endian unsigned
8restLittle-endian NBT, root compound, uncompressed

This editor shows the storage version in the file bar, preserves it, and rewrites the length for you every time you save.

Bedrock tags worth knowing

Bedrock keeps its settings flat at the root of level.dat rather than nesting them under a Data compound the way Java does, and game rules are individual tags instead of a GameRules child.

TagTypeMeaning
LevelNameStringWorld name shown in the world list and in server output
GameTypeInt0 survival, 1 creative, 2 adventure
DifficultyInt0 peaceful … 3 hard
commandsEnabledByteCheats on or off
SpawnX, SpawnY, SpawnZIntWorld spawn
RandomSeedLongWorld seed, a true 64-bit value
lastOpenedWithVersionList of IntClient or server build that last wrote the world
StorageVersionIntWorld storage revision, mirrors the header
experimentsCompoundExperimental toggles enabled for the world
keepinventory, domobspawning, …ByteGame rules, one lowercase tag each

Finding the file on each platform

  • Android: Android/data/com.mojang.minecraftpe/files/games/com.mojang/minecraftWorlds/<id>/level.dat. Newer Android releases restrict that folder — use the in-game world export, or a file manager with the right access.
  • iOS: export the world to a .mcworld from the game, open it in the Files app, and unzip it there — level.dat sits at the archive root.
  • Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Microsoft.MinecraftUWP_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalState\games\com.mojang\minecraftWorlds\<id>\level.dat.
  • Bedrock Dedicated Server: worlds/<World>/level.dat.
  • PocketMine-MP, Nukkit, PowerNukkitX: worlds/<World>/level.dat — see the server-side guide.

The world folder name is a random id, not the world name. Sort by modification time, or open a few level.dat files here and read LevelName to identify the right one.

Beyond level.dat

Bedrock keeps chunks, entities and block entities in a LevelDB database in the db/ folder, with little-endian NBT as the value of many keys. Extract a value and it opens here as Bedrock raw — no header, no compression. Structure files use the same encoding: see the .mcstructure editor. Protocol captures use the varint variant, which the editor detects as Bedrock network.
faq: Why will not my Bedrock level.dat open in NBTExplorer?
Because NBTExplorer expects Java's big-endian layout and does not know about the 8-byte Bedrock header. This editor handles both, and rewrites the header length when it saves.
Can I edit an MCPE world on my phone?
Yes. Open this page in the phone's browser, pick the file from your file manager, edit and save. The download lands in your Downloads folder; copy it back over the original.
What is the difference between storage version 8 and 10?

They mark revisions of the Bedrock world storage format; 10 is what current clients write. The editor keeps whatever value the file had rather than forcing one, because rewriting it does not migrate the world data behind it.
Does this work with .mcworld files?
Not directly — a .mcworld is a zip archive. Unzip it, edit level.dat here, put it back in the archive, and rename it back to .mcworld.
Does it work with Bedrock game rules?
Yes. Bedrock stores each rule as its own lowercase byte tag at the root — keepinventory, domobspawning, showcoordinates and so on. Set the byte to 1 or 0. The game rules guide lists them.

pocketmine-nbt-editor.body:
The duplicated-world-name problem

Every Bedrock server admin hits this. You copy worlds/hub to worlds/hub2 to make a second arena, and the console, the world manager and every plugin that reports a world name keep calling both of them hub. The folder name changed; LevelName inside level.dat did not.

The consequences are not cosmetic. Plugins that look worlds up by their internal name — teleport pads, per-world configs, region protection — can resolve to the wrong world, and world-management commands become ambiguous. Fix it by editing the tag: drop the file above and the editor jumps straight to LevelName and opens it for editing.

  1. Stop the server. A running server rewrites level.dat on save and will undo the edit.
  2. Download worlds/<World>/level.dat over SFTP or from your panel's file manager.
  3. Drop it into the editor, change LevelName to the new name, save.
  4. Upload it back over the original, keeping the old file as a backup.
  5. Start the server and check the console line that reports loaded worlds.

Core-by-core notes

CoreWorld pathNotes
PocketMine-MP (PM5)worlds/<World>/Default world set by level-name in server.properties; that value is the folder, while LevelName is what the world calls itself.
Nukkit / PowerNukkitXworlds/<World>/Same Bedrock layout; PNX adds its own settings files alongside.
Bedrock Dedicated Serverworlds/<World>/level-name in server.properties picks the folder; the header storage version is typically 10.
Cloudburst / Dragonflyworlds/<World>/Read the same level.dat; Dragonfly may keep extra state in its own database.
WaterdogPE, Geyser—Proxies. They do not own worlds; NBT only passes through them on the wire as network NBT.

Doing it without breaking production

  • Back up the whole world folder, not just level.dat. It costs seconds and it is the only thing that makes a bad edit reversible.
  • Never edit a live file over SFTP. Download, edit, upload while the server is stopped. Editing in place while the server holds the world open is how you end up with a truncated file.
  • Copying a world for a new mode? Change LevelName immediately after copying, before the server sees it, so nothing ever caches the wrong name.
  • Check the file bar after loading. It shows the detected format and the storage version — if a Bedrock file is reported as anything but Bedrock level.dat, you grabbed the wrong file or it is corrupt.
faq: Does PocketMine-MP use the same level.dat as Bedrock?
Yes. PocketMine-MP implements the Bedrock world format, so its level.dat is little-endian NBT with the 8-byte header, byte-for-byte the same shape the vanilla Bedrock server writes.
Why do two worlds show the same name in console?
Because both were copied from one folder and share a LevelName. The folder name and the tag are independent; change the tag.
Can I rename a world without restarting the server?
No. The world is loaded in memory and rewritten on save, so an edit made while it is running is discarded. Stop, edit, start.
Does this work with Nukkit and PowerNukkitX?
Yes — same format, same file path, same procedure.
How do I convert a Bedrock world to Java?
Not with an NBT editor. Byte order is the easy part; the tag layout, block palettes and chunk storage differ completely. Use a purpose-built converter, then use this editor for the leftover metadata.

Why is my .mcstructure not compressed?
Bedrock writes structure files as raw little-endian NBT with no gzip wrapper. That is normal; the editor detects it as Bedrock raw.
What does an index of -1 mean in block_indices?
It marks a position the structure does not touch, so the existing block in the world is kept when the structure is placed.
Can I resize a structure by editing size?
Not on its own — block_indices has one entry per position, so the array length has to match the new volume exactly. Changing size alone produces a file the game refuses.

The server or the player was online when you edited. Player state in memory wins on the next save.

Reading a file you did not write

Half the reason to open an NBT file is diagnosis: what version wrote this, why does this world refuse to load, what is actually inside the schematic somebody sent you. The viewer shows every tag with its exact type, so you can tell a TAG_Byte of 1 from a TAG_Int of 1 — a distinction that matters to Minecraft and that text dumps usually lose.

  • Type badges on every row — Byte, Short, Int, Long, Float, Double, Byte[], String, List, Compound, Int[], Long[].

NBT versus SNBT

The format is detected from the bytes, not the extension. A file reported as Java when you expected Bedrock is usually a file from the other edition, or a fragment that happens to parse — check the offsets reported if it warns about trailing bytes.
How big a file can it open?
Multi-megabyte documents are fine: arrays are kept in typed arrays and the tree renders lazily, so only the rows you expand exist in the page.

nbt-format.ogtitle: NBT format reference — tags, encodings, byte layout
nbt-format.desc: Reference for Minecraft's NBT format: all 13 tag types with byte layout, Java big-endian vs Bedrock little-endian vs varint network NBT, and SNBT.

nbt-format.reldesc: All 13 tag types, every encoding, byte by byte.
nbt-format.answer: NBT (Named Binary Tag) is Minecraft's binary tree format: a tag is a one-byte type, a length-prefixed name and a payload, and compounds nest until a TAG_End byte closes them. There are 13 tag types and five encodings in circulation across Java and Bedrock. This page documents all of them, and the editor above lets you check any claim against a real file.
nbt-format.body:
The 13 tag types

IdTagPayloadSNBT
0TAG_EndNone — closes a compound—
1TAG_Byte1 byte, signed −128…1271b
2TAG_Short2 bytes, signed1s
3TAG_Int4 bytes, signed1
4TAG_Long8 bytes, signed1L
5TAG_Float4 bytes, IEEE 7541.0f
6TAG_Double8 bytes, IEEE 7541.0d
7TAG_Byte_Arrayint length, then that many bytes[B;1b,2b]
8TAG_Stringunsigned short length, then UTF-8 bytes"text"
9TAG_Listelement type byte, int length, then payloads with no names[1,2]
10TAG_Compoundtype + name + payload repeated until TAG_End{a:1}
11TAG_Int_Arrayint length, then that many 4-byte ints[I;1,2]
12TAG_Long_Arrayint length, then that many 8-byte longs[L;1L,2L]

A file is a single root TAG_Compound: one type byte 0x0A, a name, then the compound's contents. Named tags appear only inside compounds — list elements carry payloads only, which is why a list is homogeneous.

Five encodings in the wild

EncodingIntegersString lengthRootUsed by
Java (classic)Big-endian fixed width2-byte big-endianNamedJava worlds, structures, schematics
Java network (1.20.2+)Big-endian fixed width2-byte big-endianNamelessJava protocol
BedrockLittle-endian fixed width2-byte little-endianNamedBedrock worlds, .mcstructure, LevelDB values
Bedrock level.datLittle-endian fixed width2-byte little-endianNamed, after an 8-byte headerBedrock world metadata
Bedrock networkZigzag varint for int and longUnsigned varintNamedBedrock protocol

In the varint encoding, TAG_Short, TAG_Float and TAG_Double stay fixed-width little-endian; only TAG_Int and TAG_Long become zigzag varints, and array and list lengths follow whatever TAG_Int does. String lengths are unsigned varints, which also lifts the 65535-byte ceiling that the fixed encodings impose.

Strings: modified UTF-8 versus UTF-8

Java serialises strings with DataOutputStream.writeUTF, which is modified UTF-8: a NUL character is written as C0 80 rather than 00, and characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane are written as two three-byte surrogate halves (CESU-8) instead of one four-byte sequence. Bedrock uses standard UTF-8. A tool that assumes one encoding for both will corrupt emoji and some CJK text on save — this editor encodes per format, which is why a world named with an emoji survives a round trip here.

Compression

NBT itself is not compressed; the container decides. Java files are usually gzip (magic 1F 8B), chunk payloads inside region files are zlib (magic 78 01, 78 9C or 78 DA), and Bedrock stores level.dat and structure files uncompressed. Detection is by magic bytes, so the same parser handles all three — and a file saved with the wrong compression is the single most common reason a hand-edited world will not load.

A minimal file, byte by byte

The canonical hello_world.nbt: a root compound named hello world holding one string tag name with the value Bananrama. In Java's big-endian encoding:

0A                          TAG_Compound
00 0B 68 65 6C 6C 6F 20 77 6F 72 6C 64   name length 11, "hello world"
   08                       TAG_String
   00 04 6E 61 6D 65        name length 4, "name"
   00 09 42 61 6E 61 6E 72 61 6D 61      value length 9, "Bananrama"
00                          TAG_End

The same document in Bedrock's little-endian encoding differs only in the byte order of the two length fields: 0B 00 instead of 00 0B. In Bedrock network NBT the lengths become single varint bytes, 0B and 04, with no padding at all. Drop any of the three into the editor above and it will tell you which one it received.

SNBT

SNBT is NBT written as text, and it is what commands consume: /data merge entity @s {Invulnerable:1b}. Type suffixes are what keep it lossless — b byte, s short, L long, f float, d double, none for int — and typed array literals are written [B;…], [I;…], [L;…]. The editor exports SNBT from any loaded file, which makes two versions of a world diffable in a normal text diff.
faq: Is there an official NBT specification?
No formal spec from Mojang. The format was documented by Notch in 2010 and has been maintained by the community since; the tag ids and layout on this page match what the game reads and writes today.
Why does Bedrock use little-endian?
Bedrock's engine is C++ and targets little-endian hardware, so it stores values in native order. Java's serialisation is big-endian because that is what the Java DataOutput contract specifies.
What is zigzag varint encoding?

A way of writing integers in as few bytes as possible while keeping negatives short: the sign is folded into the low bit, so −1 encodes as 1 and 1 encodes as 2. Bedrock's protocol uses it for ints and longs.
Can a TAG_List hold mixed types?
No. A list declares one element type and every entry has to match it. Mixed data needs a list of compounds.
What is the maximum string length?
65535 bytes in the fixed encodings, because the length field is an unsigned short. The varint network encoding has no practical limit.

guides/change-world-name.title: How to Change a Minecraft World Name (Java & Bedrock)
guides/change-world-name.ogtitle: How to change a Minecraft world name
guides/change-world-name.desc: Rename a Minecraft world properly by editing LevelName in level.dat: Java and Bedrock, single player and servers, plus the duplicate-name fix.
guides/change-world-name.keywords: how to change minecraft world name, rename minecraft world, change world name server, levelname level.dat, rename bedrock world, minecraft world still shows old name, duplicate world name server
guides/change-world-name.h1: How to Change a Minecraft World Name
guides/change-world-name.reldesc: Fix LevelName after copying a world folder.
guides/change-world-name.answer: A world's display name lives in the LevelName tag inside level.dat, not in the folder name. Renaming the folder changes nothing the game shows, which is why a copied world keeps announcing itself under the original name. Drop level.dat into the editor below — it jumps straight to LevelName — change the value, save, and put the file back.
guides/change-world-name.body:
Why renaming the folder does nothing

Minecraft treats the folder as an address and LevelName as the label. The world list, the server console, world-manager plugins and anything printing "world" to chat read the tag. So a folder copy — cp -r worlds/hub worlds/hub2 — produces two worlds that insist they are both hub, and the only fix is inside the file.

On a server the duplicate is worse than confusing. Plugins that resolve worlds by internal name can act on the wrong one: teleport pads, per-world configs, protection regions, economy multipliers. Rename the tag the moment you copy a world, before anything caches it.

Per platform

Java single player

The client offers a rename in the world options screen and it edits LevelName for you. Editing the file by hand matters when the world will not load, when you are working on a copy, or when you want the folder and the label to differ deliberately.

Java server

level-name in server.properties selects the folder to load. It does not rename anything. Change LevelName in world/level.dat for the label.

Bedrock and MCPE

The in-game world edit screen renames the world. When the world lives on a server, or you are patching an exported .mcworld, edit LevelName in level.dat directly — Bedrock stores it flat at the root, uncompressed, behind the 8-byte header the editor handles for you.

Bedrock servers (PocketMine-MP, Nukkit, BDS)

Same file, same tag, and the same warning about stopping the server first. The server page has the full workflow including the folder-copy case.

If the name does not change

  • The server was running. Its in-memory copy was written back over your file on the next save. Stop it and redo the edit.
  • You edited the wrong world. Bedrock world folders are random ids. Open the file and read LevelName to confirm you have the right one before editing.
  • You edited level.dat_old. That is the previous save, not the live file.
  • A launcher or panel caches the name. Some hosting panels show a name from their own database rather than the world file; the game itself will be correct.
  • The world will not load at all now. Restore the backup and see fixing a broken level.dat.
faq: Does renaming a world delete anything?
No. LevelName is a label. Terrain, players, inventories and entities live in other files and are untouched.
Can I use spaces, colours or emoji in a world name?

Spaces are fine. Section-sign colour codes work on some server software and show as literal characters elsewhere. Emoji survive the round trip here because the editor uses the right string encoding per edition, but consoles and log files may render them badly.
Do I have to rename the folder too?
No, and often you should not — a server's level-name setting or a plugin config may point at the folder path. Change one thing at a time.
Will players see the new name immediately?
After the world reloads, yes. Clients that cached a server list entry may need a refresh.

howto.name: Change a Minecraft world name by editing level.dat
steps: Stop the game or server
Close the world or stop the server. Minecraft rewrites level.dat on autosave and shutdown, and a running instance will overwrite the edit.
Locate level.dat
Java: world/level.dat on a server, or saves/<World>/level.dat in the client. Bedrock: worlds/<World>/level.dat on a server, or the world id folder under minecraftWorlds on a device.
Open it in the editor
Drop the file into the NBT editor. It detects the edition and encoding and jumps to the LevelName tag automatically.
Edit LevelName
Click the value, type the new name, press Enter. Keep it to plain characters if the name has to survive being printed in a console.
Save and download
Click Save & Download. The output format and compression stay exactly as the file arrived, so nothing else about the file changes.
Replace the original
Copy the downloaded file over the original, keeping a backup, then start the game or server and confirm the new name in the world list.

guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.title: Fix a Corrupted level.dat — Minecraft World Will Not Load
guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.desc: Repair a Minecraft world that will not load: restore level.dat_old, inspect the file in an NBT editor, and find what actually broke it.
guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.keywords: corrupted level.dat, minecraft world will not load, failed to load level.dat, level.dat_old restore, minecraft world corrupted fix, repair minecraft world, level.dat error server
guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.reldesc: Diagnose why a world refuses to load, and repair it.
guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.answer: A world that refuses to load usually has one of four problems: a truncated level.dat from a crash during save, the wrong compression after a hand edit, a broken Bedrock header length, or a tag whose type was changed. Drop the file below — the editor reports exactly where parsing stopped, which narrows it to one of the four in seconds.
guides/fix-corrupted-level-dat.body:
What actually breaks

SymptomCauseFix
Editor reports "Unexpected end of data"Truncated file — the process died mid-save, or the disk filled upRestore level.dat_old or a backup; the missing bytes are gone
Game says the world is corrupted, editor loads it fineWrong compression or byte order written by another toolRe-save here with the correct format for the edition
Bedrock world missing from the listHeader length no longer matches the payloadOpen and save here — the length is recalculated automatically
Server logs a class-cast or type error on loadA tag's type was changed by hand (Byte where an Int is expected)Set the tag back to the type the game expects
World loads but spawns you in a fresh worldlevel.dat was replaced by a newly generated oneRestore the backup; the chunks in region/ or db/ are usually still fine
Nothing parses, including _oldStorage failure — the filesystem returned zeros or garbage for bothRestore from an off-machine backup; check the disk before trusting the host

Salvaging a world without level.dat

The world's terrain, chests and players do not live in level.dat — they are in region/ (Java) or db/ (Bedrock). If the metadata file is beyond repair, create a fresh world with the same version and settings, then move the chunk data into it and set LevelName, spawn coordinates and game rules on the new file. You lose the metadata, not the builds. Confirm the version first: a Java world carries DataVersion, and the freshly generated file must not be older than the chunks you are importing.

Preventing the next one

  • Stop the server before copying or editing. Most corruption starts as a file copied while it was being written.
  • Snapshot on a schedule, off the machine. A backup on the same disk does not survive the storage failure that caused the problem.
  • Use save-off / save-all around live snapshots so the copy is taken against a quiesced world.
  • Watch disk space. A full disk truncates saves silently, and level.dat is written last.
  • Edit values, not structure. Renaming tags or changing their types is the one edit the game cannot forgive.
faq: What is level.dat_old?
The previous save. Minecraft renames the current file to level.dat_old before writing a new one, so it is a one-generation backup that costs nothing to try first.
Can an NBT editor repair a truncated file?
It can tell you exactly where the data stops, but the missing bytes cannot be reconstructed. A partial parse means you need a backup.
Will I lose my builds?
Not from a broken level.dat alone. Chunks live in region/ or db/; a fresh world file with the same version can adopt them.
The server says level.dat is fine but the world is empty.
Then the chunk storage is the problem, not the metadata. Check that region/ or db/ came along with the copy and that the spawn coordinates in level.dat point where you expect.

howto.name: Diagnose and repair a corrupted level.dat
steps: Back up the world folder
Copy the entire world directory before touching anything. Every step below is reversible only if you have this copy.
Try level.dat_old
Minecraft keeps the previous save as level.dat_old. Open it in the NBT editor: if it parses cleanly, copy it over level.dat and start the world.
Open the broken file
Drop level.dat into the editor. A clean parse means the file is intact and the problem lies elsewhere — chunks, mods or the server itself.
Read the error
The editor names the failure: unexpected end of data means truncation, an implausible storage version means a damaged Bedrock header, and no recognizable format means the file is not NBT at all.
Check compression and format

If it loads, look at the file bar. A Java level.dat must be saved as gzip big-endian; a Bedrock one as little-endian with the header. Re-saving with the correct settings fixes files broken by another tool.
Rebuild only what is missing
If a single tag was deleted, add it back with the correct type. If the file is truncated, prefer level.dat_old or a backup — a partially parsed file is missing data no editor can invent.

guides/edit-gamerules.title: Edit Minecraft Game Rules in level.dat — Java & Bedrock
guides/edit-gamerules.desc: Change keepInventory, doDaylightCycle, mobGriefing and other game rules by editing level.dat, for Java and Bedrock. No commands, no cheats needed.
guides/edit-gamerules.keywords: edit gamerules level.dat, keepinventory nbt, minecraft gamerules file, change gamerule without commands, bedrock gamerules level.dat, dodaylightcycle nbt, gamerules server
guides/edit-gamerules.reldesc: keepInventory and friends, without loading the world.
guides/edit-gamerules.answer: Game rules are stored in level.dat, so you can change them without loading the world or having cheats enabled — useful when a world will not start, when cheats are off, or when you are preparing a copied world before players join. Java keeps them in a GameRules compound as strings; Bedrock keeps each one as its own lowercase byte tag at the root.
guides/edit-gamerules.body:
Java: a GameRules compound of strings

In Java Edition, Data → GameRules holds one TAG_String per rule, keyed by the exact name /gamerule uses, with the value written as text: "true", "false" or a number. Rules the world has never set are simply absent and fall back to their defaults — adding the tag with the correct name and a string value works exactly like running the command.

RuleValueEffect
keepInventory"true"Keep items on death
doDaylightCycle"false"Freeze the time of day
doWeatherCycle"false"Freeze the weather
mobGriefing"false"Stop creepers and endermen changing blocks
doMobSpawning"false"Stop natural mob spawning
doFireTick"false"Fire stops spreading
commandBlockOutput"false"Silence command block chat spam
randomTickSpeed"3"Crop growth and fire spread rate
playersSleepingPercentage"50"Share of players needed to skip the night
spawnRadius"10"Spread of the spawn area

Case matters. keepinventory in a Java file is not the same tag as keepInventory and will be ignored.

Bedrock: individual lowercase byte tags

Bedrock does not group rules. Each one is a TAG_Byte at the root of level.dat, named in lowercase, holding 1 or 0 — keepinventory, domobspawning, domobloot, dodaylightcycle, doweathercycle, mobgriefing, firedamage, falldamage, drowningdamage, pvp, showcoordinates, commandblockoutput, sendcommandfeedback, naturalregeneration, tntexplodes, respawnblocksexplode, showdeathmessages, doimmediaterespawn. Numeric rules such as randomtickspeed and functioncommandlimit are TAG_Int instead.

Setting a rule that is not yet present means adding the tag with the right type: Byte for a toggle, Int for a number. A rule stored with the wrong type is ignored, or refuses to load.

When editing the file beats the command

  • Cheats are off and you do not want to toggle them on and off to run one command.
  • The world will not load — a rule such as doImmediateRespawn can be set before the first join.
  • You are preparing a template world to be copied for many servers, and want the rules baked into the copy.
  • A plugin changed a rule and you want to see what is actually stored rather than what a command reports.
  • Bulk edits. Setting a dozen rules across several worlds is faster in the file than in chat.

Stop the server first, as with any level.dat edit — a running world rewrites the file on save and will discard the change.
faq: Why is my game rule stored as a string in Java?
Java's game rule storage is string-based for every rule, including booleans and numbers. Write "true", not a byte of 1.
Why is it a byte in Bedrock?
Bedrock stores toggles as byte tags at the root and numeric rules as ints. There is no GameRules compound.
A rule is missing from the file entirely.
That means it is at its default. Add the tag with the exact name and correct type and the world will use your value.
Do game rules copy with a world folder?
Yes — they live in level.dat, so a copied world inherits them along with its stale world name.
